methodological_rigor.justification: The study is a cross-sectional diagnostic comparison of KRAS G12/G13 detection by ddPCR across four plasma fractions in 58 LUAD patients, with tumour NGS as reference and a KRASwt comparator group of equal size. The design fits the question, and endpoints (sensitivity, specificity, PPA/NPA, Cohen's kappa, MFA) are reasonable. However, no sample-size or power calculation is reported, and a critical processing asymmetry is acknowledged in the Discussion: P1/P2 were isolated and stored prior to this study while P3 was isolated after thawing — this limits internal comparability of the fractions. No multiplicity correction is reported for repeated agreement testing across four fractions and two stage strata, and 'neat' plasma was not analysed as an additional comparator (an acknowledged limitation). EV characterisation was performed in only a representative sample rather than per-case, which weakens biological inference about EV-DNA content.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The design is a single-centre, convenience-sampled, cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study with tumour NGS as reference standard; given the small (n=58), selected cohort, lack of prospective consecutive enrolment and processing asymmetry, Oxford LoE sits at 4 (low-quality diagnostic/cohort evidence) rather than 2b. Clinically, the finding that unfractionated plasma supernatant yields superior sensitivity (92.9% in late-stage KRASmt) over ultracentrifugation-derived EV fractions is practically informative — it discourages EV-based workflows for KRAS testing in LUAD using current isolation methods and reinforces cfDNA/ddPCR as the preferred approach. However, no patient-level outcomes (OS, PFS, treatment response) are evaluated, and the message largely confirms existing practice rather than changing it, so translational relevance is moderate.

reporting_quality.justification: STARD applies as this is a diagnostic accuracy study comparing an index test (ddPCR on plasma fractions) against a reference standard (tumour NGS). Many key STARD items are addressed: participant demographics (Table 1), index test methodology (ddPCR, thresholds, false-positive assay), reference standard, 2x2 agreement metrics with kappa, and discussion of indeterminate results. However, there is no explicit STARD-style flow diagram, no information on consecutive vs selected enrolment, no eligibility criteria beyond LUAD diagnosis with known KRAS status, no inter-rater reliability for thresholding, and no pre-registration or protocol reference. The blinded manuscript contains no data-availability statement, no deposited raw ddPCR data or analysis code; supplementary materials are mentioned but reproducibility details for independent replication of thresholds and MFA calculations are limited.

novelty_literature.justification: The novelty is incremental and empirical: a side-by-side comparison of three ultracentrifugation-derived fractions plus plasma supernatant for KRAS G12/G13 detection in LUAD. Directly comparable prior work in colon cancer (Choi et al. ref 17), pancreatic cancer (Allenson et al. ref 18; Bernard et al. ref 34) and NSCLC EGFR T790M (Castellanos-Rizaldos ref 19; Kim ref 29) has established EV-DNA mutation testing, and Moldovan et al. (ref 20) already reported that small EV DNA is not preferentially enriched in late-stage lung cancer. The contribution of showing SUP > EV fractions for KRAS in LUAD confirms rather than challenges this trajectory; MFA observations (higher in EV fractions than SUP) echo prior ddPCR BRAF/colorectal work (ref 35). No new assay, hypothesis, or mechanism is introduced.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written and well organised: the Introduction defines EV subtypes and MISEV2023 nomenclature, states a specific hypothesis, and situates the work; Methods are detailed for ultracentrifugation, western blot, TRPS, TEM, DNA extraction and ddPCR; Results sections are logically sequenced from EV characterisation to KRAS detection to agreement analyses; and the Discussion thoughtfully addresses discordant cases (e.g., L21), MFA interpretation and limitations. The abstract is quantitatively grounded with concrete detection rates. Figure captions are informative and standalone-interpretable. Minor issues: some long paragraphs in the Discussion could be tightened, and acronym density (SUP, P1–P3, MFA, TRPS, MISEV) is high but acronyms are generally expanded on first use.

key_strengths: Clear, hypothesis-driven comparison of four plasma fractions with KRASwt comparator group of equal size and tumour NGS as reference standard
Appropriate agreement metrics (sensitivity/specificity, PPA/NPA, Cohen's kappa) with transparent 92.9% late-stage SUP sensitivity and 100% specificity in P1
Multi-modal EV characterisation (western blot for FLOT1/CD9/albumin, TRPS, TEM) supports fraction identity claims
Thorough, candid Discussion of limitations including P1/P2 vs P3 processing asymmetry, plasma volume, and clonal haematopoiesis as a false-positive mechanism
Introduces MFA as a complementary metric and shows higher MFA in EV fractions despite lower DNA yield
key_concerns: Small, selected single-centre cohort (n=58) with no power calculation and no prospective consecutive enrolment, limiting generalisability
Critical processing asymmetry: P1/P2 were isolated pre-study and stored while P3 was isolated post-thaw, confounding fraction-to-fraction comparisons
EV characterisation performed in only a representative case rather than per-sample, weakening per-case biological inference
No multiplicity correction across repeated agreement tests spanning four fractions and two stage strata
Novelty is incremental — confirms prior cfDNA > EV-DNA findings in lung cancer (ref 20) and does not introduce new methodology
No data-availability statement or code sharing; raw ddPCR data and MFA calculation details are not deposited
chief_reviewer.rationale: A technically competent, well-written but incremental diagnostic comparison study whose main finding (plasma supernatant outperforms EV fractions for KRAS detection in LUAD) is clinically useful but confirmatory. The small, selected cohort, processing asymmetries, and lack of pre-registration/data sharing make Tier 1–2 implausible; the paper fits a Tier 3 specialty journal (e.g., Cancers, BMC Cancer-level) with minor revisions addressing STARD flow reporting, multiplicity, and data availability.
